newsitem.title: UK: LME copper under pressure following stocks rise.
newsitem.headline: LME copper under pressure following stocks rise.

text.p: London Metal Exchange (LME) copper prices were initially steady on Wednesday but moved lower in mid-morning pre-market trading on another inventory rise, traders said.

The 5,000 tonne gain in stocks pushed the net total above the psychological 200,000-tonne mark. "Another stock increase was enough to put the market on the defensive...there is little in the way of an upside manoeuvre today," one trader said.
Three months delivery was last at $2,287 a tonne in an area of light support from the 10-day moving average. This was down on Tuesday's LME kerb close of $2,300.
Traders said prices could head towards support between $2,240 and $2,250 or possibly lower.

A recent unwinding in tight nearby spreads was also likely to keep the market under pressure. Copper's cash to three months backwardation was last indicated at $80/$85, against levels of $100/$110 late on Tuesday. Last week the backwardation widened to $270.
Traders said the market would remain nervous over the movements of the spreads.
The stock increase may be due to metal being sucked in by the backwardation amid the traditionally slow summer period, they added.
Zinc maintained its recent upside drive and posted a fresh high since August 1990 of $1,554, a $10 gain from Tuesday.

Despite over-extended chart signals, traders doubted zinc would register any significant near-term losses. "There may be a period of consolidation or even a drift but overall $1,600 is soon to be seen," one trader commented.
A stocks fall of 1,400 tonnes was supportive.

Aluminium was lifted by speculative and trade buying to a near-two-month high of $1,631, a $16 gain from Tuesday. Traders said the market was targeting $1,640 and $1,650 after finally breaking above previous resistance at $1,620. A further stocks fall and signs of physical demand in the U.S. was underpinning the market.

Lead followed a small inventory fall by trading $5 higher at $650, while tin recovered from Tuesday's early March 1995 low of $5,360 on light trade buying but still looked destined to fall to $5,300 given the lack of strong consumer demand.
Alloy was indicated at $1,460/70, against $1,448/53. The higher stance of the market reflected gains in the primary market, traders said.
